film.caption: Building Blocks, 2:03. Tesa 41, November 2026
film.credit: Filmed by Bibiana Juritz and Aram Zadikian, edited by Bibiana Juritz. Sound on; English subtitles in the picture
p1: Four days before the Biennale closes, the studio is taking everything down from the shelves. For months, what was made in Tesa 41 was put away as it was finished: white plaster blocks, slabs cast with pigment, low coloured bases, wrapped in paper and stacked close to save room. This week it all comes out. On Monday the team carried the pieces to the long tables, laid them out, and began, with a tape measure, a level and Zadik Zadikian’s eye, to set each one in its place. The new film, Building Blocks, follows the work from the shelf to the table.
p2: Aram Zadikian says it plainly at the start of the film. Put away on a shelf, the work “has very little presence.” Then: “the moment that you actually take it out and you assemble it…” He leaves the sentence there. The tables behind him finish it.
fig.wrapped: Wrapped and stacked on the shelves
p3: Nothing is added between the shelf and the table. It is the same plaster, the same pigment, the same weight in the hand. What changes is the order: which piece stands beside which, what leans and what lies flat, how far apart, at what angle, facing where. Packed away, the blocks are material. Set out, they are a work.
p4: So the placing is the work, and this week it is done with care. The team measures out the spacing and runs a long level along each row; a slab is nudged a few millimetres and looked at again. Zadik moves along the tables, shifting a piece here and there. “The simpler things get, the better,” he says in the film of one arrangement. “Something peaceful and simple.”
gal.aligning: A slab set against its block
gal.around: Zadik Zadikian with the team at the tables
p5: There is an old lesson here, and an easy one to miss. A heap of bricks and a wall are the same bricks; a jumble of letters and a sentence are the same letters. What we value is seldom the stuff itself. It is the relation between the parts, the structure, and that is what we overlook most often, because we look at what a thing is made of, and not at how it is put together.
p6: Aram feels it in his hands. “I want to pick it up and handle it. There’s a toy-like element, like a building block, like a child’s toy.” Zadik answers with scale: “It’s not intimidating. This scale is very playful.” A visitor, speaking German, thought at once of the Bauhaus: the clear form against a mineral colour, and pieces you can rearrange however you like. “I think that’s great.”
fig.assembled: The formations on the studio tables
p7: As the pieces come off the shelves, out of their compact, stacked form and into the modular formations they were made for, they come alive. It is worth remembering beyond the studio. On Sunday 22 November the pavilion closes with a gathering and talks with the artist and the curator; until then the work is out, every piece in its place.
p8: The same plaster, the same pigment. Only the order has changed.
